1:
Bethphage means house of unripe young figs — an indeclinable Aramaic name, Robertson notes, found nowhere else in either Testament. It sat on the eastern slope of Olivet, a little further out from the city than Bethany yet reached first along the road. Remigius knew it as a small village of the priests, where those whose turn of temple ministration had ended lodged alongside the men replacing them, the site chosen because the Law forbade travelling above a mile on the Sabbath. Barnes measures the stage behind them at some nineteen miles up from Jericho, most of it desert. Ellicott fills the gap Matthew leaves from the other Gospels: the Lord climbing the narrow valley, the disciples behind him and the Passover pilgrims behind them, all feverish with expectation that he would at last claim his kingdom. No evangelist names the two who were sent; Ellicott and Henry guess Peter and John from the parallel errand of Luke 22:8.

Calvin reads the act as a deliberate and timed declaration. Christ had refrained from the royal title until now, taking it up only because he saw himself near the end of his course; the ride was a solemn performance to show what kind of kingdom was his. That the beast was borrowed and bare Calvin treats as the point, not the embarrassment — “a magnificent display, truly!” he says drily — since a reign unlike earthly reigns wants a procession unlike theirs. Without Zechariah 9:9 to read it by, he warns, we shall never have any relish for this history. Henry presses the same paradox from the provision itself, poor and ordinary, bespeaking a kingdom not of this world: once in his life he rode in triumph, and it was now, as he went to suffer and die. Chrysostom draws a lesson in contentment, that it is enough to employ an ass, and asks what other king entered Jerusalem so; he finds a quieter wonder in the owners’ willingness, since whoever worked on them that they did not refuse could as easily have restrained the Jews, and would not.

Among the fathers the two beasts stand for the two peoples. The ass, broken and accustomed to the yoke, is the synagogue long under the Law, and the unbroken colt the Gentiles. Hilary subdivides: the Samaritans served after a fashion of obedience and answer to the ass, the wilder nations to the colt; the two messengers he finds in Philip, through whom Samaria believed, and Peter, who brought Cornelius as the firstfruits. Jerome reaches the figure by elimination — the Lord could not have sat on both animals over so short a distance, so the history is either impossible or merely mean, and we are sent up to the figurative sense. Pseudo-Chrysostom presses the tethering: humanity bound in the chain of diabolic error until the apostles, sent as these two were, loose it by preaching. Origen carries that forward to the commission after the Ascension, where the Spirit is given the disciples that they might loose sinners. Remigius multiplies the pair into the two Testaments, the two precepts of charity, and the two orders of preachers, to the circumcision and to the Gentiles (Galatians 2:8). Raban observes that Matthew, writing for Jews, alone mentions the ass being brought, to show that the Hebrew nation, if it repent, need not despair.

Augustine handles the textual discrepancy this raises. Matthew quotes the prophet as though the she-ass were named expressly, where John does not, nor the copies of the common translation in church use; Augustine accounts for it by Matthew’s having written in Hebrew, and by the known divergences between the Septuagint and the Hebrew as rendered by men who knew that tongue. His conclusion reaches past the variant: we should not suppose that the truth is secured in sacred sounds rather than in the matter conveyed.
2:
Which village was meant is not settled. Ellicott allows either Bethany or, if the nearer of the two, Bethphage itself. Gill reports a Jewish tradition naming it Nob, a city of the priests within sight of Jerusalem, and notes that the rabbis themselves conceded Jesus took an ass from there. On the beasts the Gospels differ in a way that has to be accounted for: Mark, Luke and John mention only the colt, John calling it a young ass and the others one on which no man had ever sat (Mark 11:2; Luke 19:30), while Matthew, following Zechariah’s Hebrew, names both.

Barnes insists the choice of animal carries dignity rather than poverty. In Judea horses were kept chiefly for war, so that in peacetime kings and princes commonly rode the ass and the mule; Solomon was set on one at his enthronement (1 Kings 1:33), and the sons of the judges before him (Judges 10:4; 12:14). To ride so was not a condescension but the appropriate way for a king to ride, and the way in which the King of Zion should enter his capital.

Lightfoot turns the borrowing itself into a proof, out of the Talmud. The rabbis reckoned as a robber anyone who transgressed against the owner’s will — the man who hires a beast for the plain and takes it into the hills. Measured against that rule, what happens here looks like a miracle and not a theft: no agreement is struck and no terms are named, the animal is simply led away, and the owner is satisfied with the bare words that the Lord has need of him.

Calvin makes the verse a demonstration of divinity, and begins by clearing away the obvious reading. Christ did not want the ass to relieve the fatigue of travelling, the distance being short; as kings mount their chariots so as to be easily seen, he meant to turn the eyes of the people on himself. Two things are foretold to steady the disciples in obedience: that at the entrance of the village they will find the animal, and that once they answer that the Lord has need of it nobody will hinder them. In this way, Calvin insists, he proved his Divinity, since to know absent matters and to bend the hearts of men to compliance belong to God alone. He dismisses the patristic reading of the two beasts as ridiculous, holding with the other Gospels and with the parallelism of the Hebrew that only the colt was ridden. Clarke takes the same ground more mildly, that Christ seizes every opportunity to convince the disciples nothing is hidden from him, disposing the owner’s heart to consent before they arrive.
3:
Almost everything in the verse turns on two words, and Ellicott lays out the three senses the title might bear. It may be Lord in the highest sense, equivalent to Jehovah, so that the beasts are requisitioned for God’s service; or Christ in the particular sense in which the disciples had learned to speak of him as the Lord; or merely the master whom the disciples owned. The third he all but excludes, since the words involve a claim to more than common authority and the claim is recognised at once. Marshalling the many places where the Gospels call Jesus the Lord, he settles on the second as most in accordance with the customary language of the disciples, and adds a probable inference: if the owners of the colt were themselves disciples, they would catch the full import of the message and obey without hesitation.

Robertson presses the philology further. This is the only place in Matthew where ho kurios is applied to Jesus, setting aside the doubtful text at 28:6. He traces the word’s weight across the wider world of the first century: in the Septuagint and the papyri it names the master of a slave (Matthew 10:24), the emperor (Acts 13:27), and God himself (Matthew 11:25); Egyptians spoke of the Lord Serapis, and even Herod was hailed as Lord King. Against that background the Christians boldly claimed the word for Christ, and here Jesus is represented as using it of himself, accepting a title his followers were already giving him.

Barnes reads it down rather than up. Lord here means simply master, a title of high respect, as at Matthew 10:24, Ephesians 6:6 and 1 Peter 3:6. He agrees nonetheless about the owners’ compliance, and explains it circumstantially: they were probably acquainted with the miracles and favourably disposed, Lazarus having lately been raised, and most of the people by then reckoning him the Messiah.

Clarke holds the two notes together without choosing between them. The proprietor of all things has need of them: Christ is continually humbling himself and yet continually giving proofs of almighty power, so that belief in his divinity may be established. Slight as the phrase looks on its surface, it carries a quiet claim to lordship, and the claim is honoured the instant it is made.
4:
Robertson identifies the quotation as composite: the first line comes from Isaiah 62:11 and the remainder from Zechariah 9:9. He also settles whose words these are. John makes it plain (John 12:14 and following) that Jesus did not quote the passage himself; the citation is the Evangelist’s own comment, and the claim being made is not that Christ set out to fulfil a prophecy but that his conduct did fulfil it. Ellicott notices the formula itself, which returns to the wording of Matthew 1:22 — literally, all this has come to pass — again the writer speaking in his own person rather than reporting a word spoken in the scene.

Barnes and Clarke confirm the standing of the text being cited: the prophecy was always applied by the Jews to the Messiah. Clarke draws out the double purpose served by inspired prediction, to show the truth of prophecy in general and to designate Christ as the person intended. Gill makes the same point from the negative side. The ride was not owing to the distance, nor to weariness, for Christ was a seasoned traveller who had walked far harder roads; it answered to what was written, and to nothing else.

Ellicott adds the detail that complicates any tidy account of the scene, again out of John: at the time the disciples did not understand the significance of what they were doing as connected with the prophecy (John 12:16). The purpose lay in the mind of their Master, not in theirs. He finds it significant, too, that neither Mark nor Luke alludes to the prophecy at all, which tells against any suggestion that the participants arranged the fulfilment for effect. What the formula asserts is something harder and quieter: that the act was wrought by the deliberate will of Christ, performed by men who did not know what they were performing, and recognised only afterwards.

That later recognition is itself part of what Ellicott is pointing at. A prophecy understood in advance by everyone involved would prove little; one understood only in retrospect, by men who had been inside it without seeing it, is harder to explain away. On this reading the formula is less a flourish than an argument, and Matthew’s habit of appending it, here as in his opening chapters, marks the places where he judges the correspondence between the prophets and the life of Christ too exact to be accidental.
5:
The daughter of Zion means the people and not the buildings. Gill takes it of the inhabitants, the Jewish synagogue, and particularly of the elect among them who embraced the true Messiah; Wesley glosses it simply as the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Wesley and Robertson both mark the citation as composite and freely handled, the opening words from Isaiah 62:11 and the rest from Zechariah 9:9. Robertson and Calvin read the Hebrew’s ass, even a colt, as plain parallelism naming one animal rather than two.

The weight of the verse falls on the King’s meekness. Calvin sets him against earthly kings, whose apparel is magnificent and costly, where the prophet marks this one out by poverty, mounted on a borrowed beast of the common people. Cyril of Jerusalem makes the detail a test of identity. Many kings have come in purple, guarded by spearmen and drawn in golden chariots, so none of that distinguishes anyone; the prophet therefore gives a sign peculiar to the King, meek and riding upon an ass, and Jesus alone of kings sat upon an unyoked foal, entering Jerusalem with acclamations as a king. Wesley glories in the lowliness and in its timing: the Prince of Peace did not take a horse, a warlike animal, though he will ride on that by and by (Revelation 19:11), and the mean attitude serves the honour of his humility and the utter confusion of all worldly pomp. Clarke sums the whole entry as the triumph of humility over pride and worldly grandeur, of meekness over rage and malice.

Ellicott reads the prophecy’s larger sweep. The ideal King arrives without chariot and horse and battle bow, as a prince of peace, reviving the lowlier pageantry of the days of the Judges (Judges 10:4; 12:14), and yet the dominion promised him runs from sea to sea (Zechariah 9:10). The act strikes him as two-edged: in part an apparent concession to the fevered expectations of the disciples and the multitude, in part a protest against them, since the kingdom would prove not of this world (John 18:36).

Lightfoot adds a second fulfilment falling on the same day, since the law appointed the paschal lamb to be taken up on the tenth of the month (Exodus 12:3), and recovers the rabbis’ own puzzle over the two Messianic arrivals: Daniel’s Messiah comes with the clouds of heaven, Zechariah’s upon an ass. Their answer turned on the merit of the generation that received him. Lightfoot keeps the distinction but moves the ground of it — he comes in the clouds as judge, and on the ass not because you are, but because he is, good.
6:
Gill supplies the topography out of Mark. The colt stood tied at the door outside, in a place where two ways met, the house being just at the entrance of the village and the beast fastened in the open street (Mark 11:4). That detail matters to him: the spot was public, the animal easily seen, and it could not be taken away without being observed — as in fact the owners did observe. Ellicott fills in the same scene from Mark and Luke, which tell it more graphically: the disciples finding the colt, the question put to them by the owner and the bystanders as to why they were doing this, their answer in the very words they had been given, and their return with the animals, at which point the procession began.

Calvin makes obedience the centre of the verse, and is careful to say why it deserves the commendation Matthew gives it. The errand was not easy. The influence of Christ was not yet so great that his name alone would make an impression on strangers, and there was reason to fear the two men would be blamed for theft. What Calvin fixes on is that they make no reply and raise no objection, but go readily to the place they were sent, resting on nothing but the command and the promise. He reads that as a proof of the deference they paid their Master.

From there Calvin presses the application outward, and it is the practical weight he wants the verse to carry: that we should learn by their example to press forward through every kind of difficulty, so as to render the Lord the obedience he demands, since he will remove obstacles, open up a path, and not permit our endeavours to be unavailing. The errand, on his reading, was directed by God from first to last, and its lesson is the one the chapter opened with — that what Christ commands he also enables, and that a plain word obeyed is not to be abandoned because the obstacles look insuperable before the attempt.
7:
The harmony question comes first, and the expositors settle it the same way. Mark and Luke say plainly that Jesus rode the colt (Mark 11:7; Luke 19:35), and Robertson holds that Matthew does not contradict them: the pronoun in set him thereon refers to the garments thrown across the colt, not to two animals. Ellicott agrees, picturing the Lord riding the colt while the ass followed or went along at his side. Clarke adds the textual evidence. Against epano auton, upon them, the Codex Bezae and several Old Latin copies read ep’ auton, upon him; Clarke judges this most likely the true reading, since we can scarcely suppose he rode both by turns, still less both at once. Robertson notes that the garments were the outer himatia, and that the verb for his seating is an ingressive aorist: he took his seat.

The laying down of the garments is read as homage with a precedent. Clarke explains it as a custom observed when the people found that God had appointed a man to the kingdom, and points to the captains under Jehu, who spread their garments on the steps and cried that Jehu was king (2 Kings 9:13). The disciples, having no saddle, did the same office in miniature, and in setting him on the clothes acknowledged him their king.

Clarke also records the older allegory, though he keeps it at arm’s length. The ass that was tied stands for the Jews bound under the yoke of the law, the colt that had never been tied for the Gentiles who were not under the law, and Christ’s sitting on both signifies his subjecting Jew and Gentile alike to the sway of his evangelical sceptre. Clarke declines either to press this or to dismiss it, closing with the proviso that he who can receive the saying may receive it. The two readings therefore stand side by side without being reconciled: the grammarians prefer the plain sense of a single colt and the manuscript evidence that supports it, while the older interpreters hear in the pair of animals the gathering in of two peoples. What neither side disputes is the gesture, which belongs to the enthronement of a king and was understood as such by everyone present.
8:
The crowd was a confluence rather than a single body. Part had come up with Jesus from Jericho and Galilee; part streamed out from Bethany, excited by the recent raising of Lazarus (John 12:17); part poured out of Jerusalem carrying palm branches to meet him (John 12:13). Spreading garments was a recognised act of homage to a king, and Wesley and Ellicott both reach for the captains under Jehu (2 Kings 9:13); Ellicott adds a pagan parallel in Agamemnon walking on costly carpets in Aeschylus. Barnes expounds the palm at length, an emblem of joy and victory used by Jews and Romans alike as a symbol of peace (1 Maccabees 13:51; Revelation 7:9), and abundant about Jericho, the city of palm trees. Robertson, reading the change of tenses, traces the growing enthusiasm of the crowd: only the greater part did this, and they picked the garments up again after the colt had passed and spread them once more ahead.

Lightfoot supplies the ritual background and corrects the picture most readers form. The people did not, he argues, strew garments and boughs under the feet of the ass to be trodden on, which might have thrown down the rider; by the wayside they made little tents and tabernacles of clothes and boughs, after the custom of the feast of Tabernacles, carrying the lulab, the young branches of palms prescribed at Leviticus 23:40. Clarke gathers the rabbinic legends that had settled round the animal: that it was the colt created in the twilight of the sixth day, ridden by Abraham and by Moses, and the one on which the Messiah should ride.

Calvin weighs what the homage was worth, and begins by conceding how little it looks. The scene might be thought a game of little children, obscure persons bestowing an empty title of king on a man with nothing to show for it. His answer is that they did this in good earnest, and that Christ looked on them as fit heralds of his kingdom. He presses the comparison into the present: even now Christ commissions from the heavenly throne obscure men, by whom his majesty is celebrated in a despicable manner. As to the branches, Calvin denies that any ancient and solemn rite was being observed, judging rather that a few acted by a sudden movement of the Spirit and the rest of the multitude imitated what they had begun.
9:
Hosanna is a Hebrew imperative, which Barnes and Ellicott render Save now, we beseech thee. Robertson traces it into liturgical use from Psalm 118:25–26, within the great Hallel (Psalms 113–118) sung at the feasts. Clarke connects it with the ritual of Tabernacles, when the people circled the altar carrying branches and on the eighth day raised the hosanna rabba, the Great Hosanna. Son of David names the Messiah, and Robertson draws the conclusion the title forces: the crowd were now proclaiming Jesus as the Messiah, and he let them do it. The next clause comes from the same Psalm, and Barnes glosses the coming as coming by the authority of the Lord, while Hosanna in the highest asks salvation from the highest heaven, an echo of the angels’ song at the Nativity (Luke 2:14).

Ellicott gathers the whole range of cries the four Gospels preserve — Blessed be the King, Blessed be the kingdom of our father David in Mark, Peace in heaven and glory in the highest in Luke — and sets against that noise the silence of Christ, who would not rebuke the shout when the Pharisees asked him to (Luke 19:39) and yet wept over the city’s coming fall (Luke 19:41).

Calvin reads the cry as inspired prayer rather than enthusiasm. The words were not rashly bestowed on Christ; the people followed with reverence a form of prayer which the Holy Spirit had prescribed to the whole Church by the mouth of the Prophet. The Psalm spoke first of David’s kingdom, but Calvin holds that it looks principally to the eternal succession, which is Christ’s. He draws the line forward to the Lord’s Prayer: when we say Thy kingdom come, the same thing is conveyed which the psalm expresses more clearly. That mean and uneducated men could frame such a petition proves to him that the doctrine was at that time well known.

Wesley is warier about how much the singers understood. They cried out probably from a Divine impulse, for certainly most of them did not understand the words they uttered. He also marks the change in Christ’s own practice: having until now restrained every public token of honour, he suffered these, so that they might stand as a public testimony against the wickedness of men who within four or five days exchanged their hosannas for the cry to crucify him.
10:
The verb Matthew chooses is strong. Robertson and Clarke render it that the city was shaken, as by an earthquake: even Jerusalem, frozen with religious formalism, was stirred with popular enthusiasm as by a mighty wind. Ellicott sets the date and the demography behind the stir — the beginning of the Paschal week, the city filled with pilgrims from many lands, to whom such a triumph came as a strange prelude to the usual order of the feast, so that they asked what it meant. Jerome and Henry both fasten on what the question exposes, the ignorance of the holy city: the Holy One unknown in the holy city, with the common multitude knowing him better than the scribes and Pharisees and rulers did. Origen hears beneath the question the words of the Psalm, Who is this King of glory (Psalm 24:8).

Calvin is interested in the publicity of the scene and why Matthew bothers to record the commotion at all: to inform us that the transaction did not take place secretly, and that the priests and scribes were not ignorant of it. Their failure to intervene he refuses to read as indifference. They abstained from opposing it not because they treated him with contempt, but because they were restrained by secret fear, God having struck them with such alarm that they dared attempt nothing. The question itself, though, betrays the careless indifference of the city’s own inhabitants, set over against the piety of those who had only just arrived in it.

The older interpreters look past the question to what Christ does next, which is to enter the temple. Pseudo-Chrysostom finds in it the part of a good Son, to haste to his Father’s house, and the part of a good physician, to apply himself first to the source of the sickness; his reason is that when the priesthood is sound the whole Church flourishes, and when it is corrupt faith is impaired. Raban marks the timing instead. The entry fell five days before the passover, answering the law’s command that the paschal lamb be taken into the house on the tenth day (Exodus 12:3), which he offers as evidence of the correspondence between the Old Testament and the New not only in things but in seasons. So the King acclaimed outside the walls and unrecognised within them goes to purify his Father’s house.
11:
Gill weighs the answer as a creditable one, observing that the common people knew Christ better than the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the scribes and Pharisees and rulers of the people; the crowd’s testimony, however humble, outran the city’s blank ignorance. To call him the Prophet was, Clarke argues, to name that prophet whom Moses spoke of, the one God promised to raise up like unto himself (Deuteronomy 18:18), so that every expression of the multitude plainly intimated that they received him as the promised Messiah. Jerome reads the title the same way and notes the sequence of thought: they begin with the lesser that they may come to the greater, hailing him as the Prophet like to Moses, with the Greek marking the title by its definite article. Henry adds the change this represents, that Christ had hitherto been known chiefly as a prophet, and only now is attended as a King.

The flaw in the confession is the epithet of Nazareth, which helped confirm some in their prejudices against him by seeming to disqualify him from the office. Wesley meets the objection directly: if he was of Nazareth he could not be the Messiah, but those who earnestly desired to know the truth would not stumble at it, for on inquiry they would find he was not of Nazareth but of Bethlehem. Clarke looks ahead to the sequel and marvels at the fickleness of the same mouths, finding it strange that these very people should within about five days change their hosannas for Away with him, crucify him.

Two things are therefore true of the answer at once. The despised crowd sees further than the learned city, and yet its sight is dim enough to be swept within the week into the opposite cry. Clarke’s remedy is implied by his own objection and Wesley’s answer to it: a confession resting on the mood of a morning will not survive the week, where one resting on the searching of the Scriptures is led past Nazareth to Bethlehem, and past the prophet to the King. Gill’s comparison cuts the same way, since what commends the multitude is not the depth of what they knew but their readiness to say it aloud, in a city whose teachers would not.
12:
The traffic stood in the outer Court of the Gentiles, which Barnes calls the least sacred part of the temple and maps within the whole sacred enclosure. There pilgrims bought oxen, sheep and doves for sacrifice, and the money-changers exchanged foreign coin for the Jewish half-shekel of the temple tax (Exodus 30:13). Lightfoot describes a constant market in the temple shops, swollen now by the nearing Passover, and tells the story of Bava Ben Buta importing three thousand sheep. Ellicott explains where the money went: the priests found their profit in charging rent, and the changers took the usual agio. He also warns against judging the arrangement too harshly from a distance, recalling St Paul’s cathedral in Elizabeth’s day, through which mules and horses laden with market produce were led as a matter of every-day occurrence. On the dove-sellers he notices a sharper edge in Christ’s treatment: at the first cleansing the dealers had merely been bidden to depart (John 2:16), where now, as if indignant at their return, he overturns their seats as well.

That this was a second cleansing most of the expositors accept. Chrysostom argues from the differing replies that John’s account belongs to a separate and earlier occasion (John 2:14), and presses the consequence as a heavier charge against the Jews, who having been reproved twice continued in their trafficking. Robertson draws the wearier moral, marvelling how short a time the work of reformers lasts. Barnes and Ellicott add from Mark that the purging was probably completed on the day after the entry rather than within the first hour of it.

Henry treats the deed as an exercise of kingship, and makes a large claim for it: this was the only act of regal authority and coercive power that Christ did in the days of his flesh. From it he derives the pattern of all reformation, that the eye must be upon the scripture, corrupted ordinances being reduced to their primitive institution. Calvin reaches the same conclusion about what the act declared — that Christ showed himself both King and High Priest, presiding over the temple — and then guards it against misuse, lest any private individual think himself entitled to act in the same manner. The godly must burn with grief at the pollutions of the church; but lacking public authority they are to oppose by their tongue those vices they cannot remedy with their hands. Wesley notes the sharper language used this second time, and that the trade occupied the outer court, where the Gentiles used to worship.
13:
The citation is a free combination of two prophets, as Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Calvin and Wesley all recognise: the house of prayer from Isaiah 56:7, the den of thieves from Jeremiah 7:11. Henry draws out the first by subordinating the whole ceremonial system to it: all those institutions were meant to be subservient to moral duties, so that the house of sacrifices was to be a house of prayer, prayer being the substance and soul of all those services. Calvin presses instead on the word Isaiah attaches to it, that the temple should be a house of prayer for all nations. He takes this as foretelling the calling of the Gentiles, and concedes it was never literally fulfilled by all nations going up to Jerusalem; it was realised when out of Zion went forth the law (Isaiah 2:3; Micah 4:2) and the living waters flowed out from the temple to water the world (Ezekiel 47:9; Zechariah 14:8).

Ellicott and Clarke give the second phrase its pictorial force. Palestine swarmed with bands of outlaw brigands who haunted the limestone caverns of Judaea, as David did at Adullam (1 Samuel 22:1), and Ellicott’s point is that their wrangling over booty was reproduced in the Temple and mingled with the Hallelujahs of the Levites. Robertson locates the theft precisely, in the charging of exorbitant prices. Calvin reads Jeremiah’s word as aimed past the traders at the hypocrites who, through confidence in the temple, allowed themselves greater liberty in sinning, making dissembled piety the cloak and cover of iniquity; Henry says the same and adds that robbing God is the worst theft of all (Malachi 3:8).

Barnes asks the question the narrative leaves open — why the traders submitted to one man — and answers it from four directions. They were overawed by his authority, reproved by their own consciences, faced by a people who generally held him to be the Messiah, and aware that a prophet had a right to order the various affairs relating to external worship. Mark and Luke record what the rulers did instead of submitting: stung, they sought how they might destroy him, and were held back only by fear of the people (Mark 11:18). Clarke turns the charge forward onto the church of every age, where those who enjoy the revenues and neglect the service of it are thieves and robbers in more senses than one.
14:
Henry sets the two halves of the day against each other. Having driven out the buyers and sellers, Christ invited the blind and lame in; the temple was profaned and abused when it was made a market-place, and graced and honoured when it was made a hospital, since to be doing good in God’s house better becomes it than to be getting money there. Clarke turns the same contrast into a test that outlasts the scene: the church or chapel in which the blind and the lame are not healed has no Christ in it, and is not worthy of attendance.

Ellicott takes up the old difficulty raised by 2 Samuel 5:8, where the Septuagint reading would seem to shut the blind and the lame out of the house of the Lord. His answer is textual and historical at once: the decisive words are not in the Hebrew, and there is no evidence from Jewish writers that the blind and the lame were ever excluded. What the two passages really set side by side, he argues, is the contrast between the hasty, passionate words of a conquering king and the tender compassion of the Son of David, to whom the blind and the lame were objects not of antipathy but of pity. They were accustomed to throng the temple gates as beggars, as Acts 3:2 shows, and now followed the great Healer inside.

Calvin fastens on the evidential weight of the cures, and ties them to the act that preceded them. So that the authority Christ had claimed for himself might not be suspected of rashness, he supported it by miracles; by healing he proclaimed that the rights and honour of Messiah truly belonged to him, since it is by these marks that the prophets describe him. Barnes supplies the mark in question from Isaiah 35:6. On Calvin’s reading the healings function as God’s own endorsement from heaven of the praises the people had been raising in the street. He then repeats the caution he had entered over the cleansing: not every one of the people is called to imitate this action of Christ, lest a man inconsiderately raise himself to the throne of the Messiah. Henry weighs the works against the words and gives the works the greater evidential force, finding in them the fulfilment of the promise that the glory of the latter house should exceed the glory of the former.
15:
Henry explains the indignation by what the rulers could not do: they could not deny the miracles to be true, and were therefore cut to the heart. Clarke sharpens the motive and generalises it. They were incensed that the temple had been purified, a work they should have done themselves, and he adds the uncomfortable observation that the priesthood itself, in all corrupt times, has ever been the most forward to prevent a reform in the Church, fearing that a reformer would find them no better than money-changers. Both the cures and the shouting galled them. Ellicott identifies the men precisely, the heads of the twenty-four courses together with Annas and Caiaphas.

Robertson and Ellicott both note that the criers were boys, strictly speaking, perhaps between seven and fourteen, who had caught the enthusiasm of the crowd. Lightfoot supplies the custom that makes their part in it unremarkable: children were taught from their first infancy to manage the bundles, to shake them, and in shaking to sing Hosanna, so that as soon as a little child could be taught to handle a bundle he was bound to carry one. The cry was therefore no novelty in itself, and Clarke draws the conclusion that follows — the rulers were exasperated only because a person was being celebrated against whom they had a rooted hatred.

Calvin locates the grievance in wounded authority rather than in doctrine. The priests contended for their own standing, and it was no slight diminution of their power if the people were at liberty to bestow on Christ the title of King. He also reconstructs the reasoning they thought sound: that it was foolish and unreasonable for the people to confer the title of Messiah on a man whom they, the teachers, did not treat with any respect. Calvin’s answer turns that argument against them. Had they done their duty as the messengers of the Lord of hosts (Malachi 2:7), it is they who should have led the people to him; having basely extinguished the light of truth, they cannot now complain that others carry it. Hence the reply he reads into the episode, that God will sooner give mouths and tongues to stones than allow the kingdom of his Son to be without witnesses — which Calvin calls no slight consolation, since the malice of the great cannot silence the praise of Christ.
16:
Ellicott reconstructs why the question was asked at all, and makes it an ambush rather than an inquiry. The priests had probably remained in the Temple and had not heard the Hosannas raised on the Mount of Olives, so the children’s shouting took them by surprise; they turned to the Teacher to ask whether he accepted it, which is to ask whether he had really entered the Temple claiming to be the expected Christ. The single word of assent removes even the suspicion of the contrary.

The answer cites Psalm 8:2, and Barnes and Robertson both note that it follows the Septuagint, which has perfected praise where the Hebrew reads ordained strength. The point of the quotation survives either rendering, since on both the praise of children is something God himself has established. Robertson adds that the verb rendered perfected is the one used of mending nets at Matthew 4:21, and calls the citation a stinging rebuke. Clarke argues from the Psalm’s use elsewhere that it was never merely devotional: it is applied to Christ three times in the Epistles (1 Corinthians 15:27; Ephesians 1:22; Hebrews 2:6), which proves it a prophetic psalm relating to the Messiah. Ellicott remarks on the form of the question, have ye never read, which was Christ’s frequent reproach to interpreters who spent their lives in the study of the Law and yet perverted its meaning.

Calvin draws out what the Psalm is actually claiming. David means that though every tongue were silent, God needs no other orators to proclaim his power than mere infants still hanging on their mothers’ breasts. In themselves such infants say nothing; it is the wonderful providence of God shining in them that serves the purpose of splendid and powerful eloquence, for whoever considers how a child is formed in the mother’s womb must be carried away into admiration of him. Calvin completes the argument by analogy: as the dumb sun and moon are said to have a loud and distinct voice for singing God’s praises (Psalm 19:1), it is no strange thing that Christ should make children sing his. Henry puts the same thought in the Psalm’s own terms, that praise is perfected out of the mouth of such, God ordaining strength from babes and sucklings and perfecting his strength in weakness.
17:
Pseudo-Chrysostom finds a rule of wisdom in the withdrawal. A bad man is better overcome by giving way to him than by replying to him, since wickedness is not instructed but stimulated by reproof; the Lord accordingly sought by withdrawing himself to check those whom his words could not check. Henry reaches the same reading by a different route, taking Christ to have left the priests as incorrigible, and finding two motives in the departure: prudence, lest they seize him before his hour was come, and justice, because they had forfeited the favour of his presence. His warning is drawn from the second — that by repining at Christ’s praises we drive him from us.

Clarke marks the daily pattern this begins. From that day until his death Christ spent not one night in Jerusalem, going out every evening to Bethany and returning to the city each morning (Luke 21:37), partly to avoid the snares laid for him and partly to take away all suspicion of his affecting the regal power. The village lay about two miles from Jerusalem, past Mount Olivet (John 11:18). Robertson and Ellicott note the irony in the name, which means house of depression or misery, while the home of Martha and Mary and Lazarus was for Jesus a house of solace and comfort through this week of destiny; and both find the suppression of those friends’ names in the first three Gospels every way significant.

Jerome reads the lodging as evidence of poverty. Christ was in such poverty that he had found in all that city neither entertainer nor abode, and made his home in a little village, in the house of Lazarus and his sisters. Origen takes the name itself for the lesson, Bethany being the house of obedience, that is, the Church, where Christ had taken rest: every man obedient to the word of God is Bethany, and Christ abides in him, while the wicked and the sinners he leaves. So the King who has purged the temple, healed in it and silenced the proud goes out of the unbelieving city to lodge with the obedient — and Origen’s reading sets up the morning that follows, where the same fathers find in the barren fig-tree the synagogue Christ came to full of leaves and void of fruit.
18:
Henry reads the return itself as the first thing worth noticing. Some think Christ had lodged outside the walls because none of his friends there durst entertain him for fear of the great men; yet, having work to do in the city, he returned. The rule Henry draws from it is that we must never be driven off from our duty either by the malice of our foes or the unkindness of our friends, and he presses the comparison with Paul, who went bound in the spirit to Jerusalem knowing that bonds and afflictions awaited him there (Acts 20:22).

That he hungered is taken by all of them as plain proof of his manhood, and each explains the circumstance differently. Clarke and Ellicott suppose that neither he nor his disciples had anything but what they got from public charity. Robertson puts it more bluntly, that Jesus had spent the night out of doors and so had no breakfast. Ellicott infers from Luke that the greater part of the night had gone in solitary prayer, which accounts for the exhaustion that sought food wherever there might seem even a chance of finding it. Henry turns the hunger inward, finding that the zeal of God’s house did even eat him up, and that his meat and drink was to do his Father’s will.

Calvin faces the difficulty the verse raises without softening it. Christ did not pretend hunger but actually felt it, since we know that he voluntarily became subject to the infirmities of the flesh. The harder question is how he could be mistaken in seeking fruit on a tree that had none, and Calvin gives two answers rather than one: as man he did not know at a distance what kind of tree it was, though it is also possible he approached it on purpose with full knowledge of the result. What Calvin will not allow is that the curse came from temper. It was not the fury of passion that led him to curse the tree, which would have been not merely unjust but a childish and ridiculous revenge; rather, as hunger was troublesome to him according to the feeling of the flesh, he determined to overcome it by an opposite affection, the desire to promote the glory of the Father (compare John 4:34). On that reading the hunger is not an interruption of his work but the occasion of it, giving him opportunity to perform a miracle, to teach his disciples, and to set before them an outward sign of the end awaiting hypocrites.
19:
The expositors begin by clearing Christ of any wrong to an owner. The tree stood in the way, by the roadside, and Gill, Barnes and Clarke all treat it as common property with no owner, so that no injury was done to any person; Lightfoot classes it among the wild figs held by common right. They then meet the difficulty Mark raises, that the time of figs was not yet (Mark 11:13). Ellicott answers from horticulture: the fig bears two or three crops a year, and this tree, in full foliage and so far in advance of its fellows, might fairly be expected to carry the first ripe fruit (Hosea 9:10; compare Song of Solomon 2:13). Robertson supplies the botanical detail that makes the expectation reasonable, since the early figs start in spring before the leaves, so that there should have been fruit on a tree already carrying a crop of leaves. The leaves, in short, made a promise the tree could not keep.

Barnes is careful about the word curse, which he says does not imply here anger, or disappointment, or malice, but only devoting to destruction, the sense in which the Jews commonly used it (Hebrews 6:8). Calvin reaches the same reading and sharpens it by contrast: the tree was condemned to barrenness by the same voice that elsewhere bestows fertility. Both note from Mark that the withering, though immediate — on the spot, as Robertson renders the adverb — was not observed until the following day.

Most of them take the tree for a sign, and differ only in how far to press it. Henry reads it twice over, first of hypocrites in general, since Christ looks for the power of religion from those who profess it and finds leaves only, and then of the nation and people of the Jews in particular, who called Abraham their father but did not do the works of Abraham. Ellicott sees the parable of Luke 13:6 embodied here, the doom then deferred now falling. Barnes alone holds back, allowing that the incident makes a good illustration of the destruction of the Jewish people while insisting there is not the least evidence that our Saviour intended it as such — a caution worth recording precisely because the rest of the tradition runs the other way.
20:
The chronology has to be settled first, and Gill, Barnes, Ellicott and Wesley all settle it from Mark 11:20: the disciples saw the withered tree the next morning as they returned from Bethany, and it was Peter who, as spokesman of the rest, drew his Master’s attention to it. Matthew means only to say that this was said to Christ, where Mark tells us which of them said it. Whether the withering was watched as it happened or inferred from its completeness when seen, Ellicott leaves open; on either account what the disciples marvelled at was the suddenness of the thing. Gill adds the detail Mark gives of what they actually saw, a tree dried up from the roots, and observes that they had heard the word spoken against it the day before without taking notice of the withering at the time.

Henry presses the manner of the judgment rather than its speed. There was no visible cause of the fig tree’s withering, but a secret blast, a worm at the root; and not the leaves only but the body of the tree withered in an instant and became like a dry stick. From that he draws his comparison, that Gospel curses are the most dreadful of all because they work insensibly and silently, by a fire not blown yet effectually. The hypocrite’s profession may stand green a while on the same terms, and, having no root in itself, withers from within once the curse has fallen on it.

Clarke turns the marvel on the people doing the marvelling. We often say of our neighbours how suddenly this man died, and who could have expected it so soon; but who takes warning by these examples, when what we say today of others may be said tomorrow of ourselves? The response he urges is the disciples’ own astonishment turned into petition — be ye also ready, and Lord, increase our faith — which is also how the passage moves into the teaching on faith and prayer that follows. The two notes the verse strikes are therefore struck together: wonder at a power needing no visible instrument, and the self-examination that wonder ought to provoke, lest the barren tree prove a portrait of the onlooker as much as of the nation under judgment.
21:
Clarke, Barnes and Ellicott agree that removing mountains was a proverbial form of speech for overcoming great difficulties. Lightfoot supplies the usage itself out of the rabbis, among whom the learned were styled rooters up of mountains. Rabh Joseph is Sinai, runs the saying, and Rabbah is a rooter up of mountains, a compliment paid to a piercing judgment. Christ therefore deservedly uses the phrase to set forth the power of faith. Ellicott argues that the form of words excludes a literal fulfilment, as the parallel at 1 Corinthians 13:2 shows, and that the demonstrative points at the Mount of Olives in order to give greater vividness to an illustration the disciples would readily understand (compare Matthew 17:20). Robertson glosses the verb for doubting as to waver, the opposite of faith, and notes that many take the blighted tree itself for an emblem of the Jewish people, with a great show of religion and no fruit. Barnes allows that if they had the faith of miracles the literal removal would be as easy for God as healing the sick, but thinks Christ rather referred to the difficulties and trials of their coming ministry.

Calvin uses the verse to define faith, beginning with what faith does rather than what it is. Faith, if we have any, breaks out immediately into prayer and penetrates into the treasures of the grace of God; and Christ joins the two deliberately, since had he only promised that we shall have whatever we wish, some would have thought the promise presumptuous. The passage therefore exhibits both the power and the nature of faith, which Calvin describes as a certainty, relying on the goodness of God, that does not admit of doubt. He will not acknowledge as believers any but those fully convinced that God is reconciled to them, and against the doubt he says his opponents mingle with faith he sets Paul’s boldness to approach God with confidence (Ephesians 3:12). Having opened the promise that wide, he immediately fences it. Christ does not give a loose rein to the wishes of men but places prayers after the rule of faith, so that the Spirit holds all our affections by the bridle of the word of God.
22:
The point of the saying, Robertson says, is faith in the efficacy of prayer, which is the same lesson the figure of the mountain had just taught. Gill takes the all things broadly, extending it past miracles to any other thing which may be for the honour of God, the interest of religion, the spreading of the Gospel, the enlargement of the kingdom of Christ, their own spiritual good and the welfare of immortal souls. Clarke fits the promise into an order of salvation, where a conviction of the want of mercy begets prayer, or warm desires, which the soul then puts into words, believes the word of promise, and so receives, according to the merciful promise of God, the salvation it requires.

Ellicott supplies the qualification without which the promise cannot stand. As at Matthew 7:7, there is an implied condition that what is asked be in harmony with the laws and will of God; and his reason is worth noting, since it is not arbitrary. Were it otherwise the thing would not be asked in faith at all, because every true prayer involves the submission of what it asks to the divine judgment. He then adds a christological observation that reaches beyond the verse: the promise suggests, as John 11:42 states outright, that our Lord’s miracles were less frequently wrought by an inherent supernatural virtue — though that also distinctly appears, as with the woman with the issue of blood (Luke 8:46) — than by power received from the Father in answer to his own prayers.

Barnes presses a caution in the opposite direction, against over-claiming. The promise was evidently a special one, designed specially for the apostles and given them in regard to working miracles, and to them it was true; but we have no right to apply it to ourselves without limit, nor to turn it from its original meaning. Gill’s wide application and Ellicott’s qualifying clause together leave the promise open and yet bounded, so that prayer offered in real faith, and within the will of God, is never denied. Henry puts the same thing positively: the believing expectation shall not be frustrated.
23:
Ellicott identifies the challengers as representatives of the three constituent elements of the Sanhedrin, the chief priests and elders with the scribes whom Luke adds. Henry separates the jurisdictions, the chief priests belonging to the ecclesiastical court and the elders to the civil (2 Chronicles 19:8), now combining against him. Pseudo-Chrysostom traces the motive to jealousy, because they had seen Christ entering the Temple in great glory; Chrysostom notices the tactic, that being unable to detract from his miracles they bring their matter of blame from his forbidding men to sell in the Temple.

The two questions are distinct barbs. Jerome takes the first as a renewal of the old slander (Matthew 12:24) that what he does is of the Devil, and the second as a most clear denial of the Son of God, since it supposes him to work not by his own but by others’ strength. Pseudo-Chrysostom hears in the second an assumption about how authority is conferred at all, that there are many persons who give power to men: thou art not come of a priestly family, the Senate has not conferred this power on thee, neither has Caesar. His explanation of the blindness is shrewder than the taunt — every man judges of others by himself, and he who is not a Priest of God thinks no man’s Priesthood to be of God. Ellicott fills in the institutional background, where the right to teach was conferred by the scribes on a man who had studied at the feet of a master and was marked by the delivery of a key; the question therefore implied that they knew the Prophet of Nazareth had never been so admitted.

Calvin allows the challenge a plausible surface, since a man ought not of his own accord to intermeddle with the prophetical office but should wait for the calling of God (Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7:21). What condemns it is its timing and its malice, the divine majesty of Christ having already been attested by so many miracles. Origen offers a subtler account of what they were fishing for: knowing that particular powers are many, they wished to learn the special degree of the power in Christ, who wrought all in one power received of the Father; and because they were not worthy to hear such mysteries he answers them with a question instead. Henry draws the question back on anyone who exercises office, since those who take upon them to act with authority should ask themselves who gave them that authority — though these men asked it only to ensnare and entangle him.
24:
Barnes holds that Christ was under no obligation to give them an answer, for the plain reason that they well knew by what authority he did this: he had worked miracles openly and had claimed to be the Messiah. Clarke puts the same judgment in terms of evidence already supplied, since Christ had given them such proofs of his Divine mission as could not possibly be exceeded, so that any further profession would have been in vain before men obstinately prejudiced. Instead of refusing outright he took the wise in their own craftiness. Henry treats the manoeuvre as a model of prudence: those who go as sheep in the midst of wolves must be wise as serpents, and are to give a reason of the hope that is in them with prudent caution, lest truth be damaged or themselves endangered.

Robertson notes that the Greek asks for a single word, and that the word is the whole point, since the answer to Christ’s question will carry the answer to theirs — the only human ecclesiastical authority Jesus had came from John. Ellicott develops the logic of precedent. As one who taught having authority and not as the scribes (Matthew 7:29), Christ challenges their right to interrogate him at all, and the test is whether they had ever exercised that right responsibly with the Baptist. If they had left his claim unquestioned, or had shrunk from confessing the result of their inquiry, they had virtually abdicated their office, and had no right in logical consistency to interrogate another teacher now.

Wesley states the chain of reasoning without ornament. The baptism, that is, the whole ministry of John, was it from heaven or from men? By what authority did he act and teach, and did man or God give him that authority? Was it not God? And if so, the consequence was clear, for John testified that Jesus was the Christ. The counter-question is therefore not a dodge but a question already containing, for any honest mind, the answer to their own, since the forerunner sent from heaven had pointed to the very man whose authority they were now pretending to doubt. Clarke’s point about obstinate prejudice and Ellicott’s about abdicated office meet here: the men asking had disqualified themselves by their own earlier silence.
25:
Henry, Gill, Barnes and Calvin all take the baptism of John to stand for his whole ministry, preaching as well as baptizing. Calvin explains what the question was designed to do: to convict them, by their own reply, of having impudently pretended ignorance of a matter with which they were well acquainted. John had been sent as Christ’s herald (Malachi 3:1; Luke 7:27), claiming nothing for himself but to prepare the way of the Lord, and had pointed out Christ with the finger. The consequence Calvin draws is tight: it was impossible to acknowledge John a servant of God without acknowledging that Christ was himself the Lord. The first horn of the dilemma was therefore fatal, since to confess the baptism from heaven was to invite the ready reply, why then did ye not believe him.

Robertson catches the tense Matthew uses of their deliberation, a picturesque imperfect describing their hopeless quandary. Ellicott finds the self-communing eminently characteristic of men who had halted between two opinions: once they came to John’s baptism (Matthew 3:7), and once they said he had a devil (Matthew 11:18), watching all the while the ebb and flow of a public reverence which the death of John had only deepened. Their reluctance had a specific cause, and Ellicott names it: to admit his prophetic character would have involved the necessity of accepting the testimony he had borne to Jesus.

Calvin draws a standing principle out of the exchange. The question Christ meant to force was whether John was a true and lawful prophet of God or an impostor, and the lesson is that no doctrine and no sacrament ought to be received among the godly unless it is evident that it has come from God. The whole government of the Church depends on the will of God in such a manner that men have no right to introduce anything from themselves — a thrust Calvin aims at the pretended sacraments which men of no authority have foolishly introduced. What disqualifies the priests, on his reading, is not ignorance but motive: they do not inquire what is true, choosing rather to shuffle than to acknowledge what they know to be true, so that their tyranny may not be impaired.
26:
Barnes states the danger in the plainest terms, that they feared the people would stone them, as Luke reports. To profess so unpopular a sentiment as that all John did was imposture would probably have ended in tumult and perhaps in their own death, since all held John to be a prophet (Matthew 14:5). Gill specifies what the second answer would have committed them to: that John’s ministry was merely human, something he took up of himself. That was the only alternative to confessing it divine, and it was an alternative they dared not speak aloud.

Henry draws out two things the admission lays bare. The first is that the people had truer sentiments of John than the chief priests and the elders had, so that the common sort, despised by their rulers as men who knew not the law and were cursed, in fact knew the gospel and were blessed. The second is a judgment on the rulers themselves: that the chief priests and elders stood in awe of the common people is evidence that things were in disorder among them, the government having become obnoxious to the hatred and scorn of those it governed, which Henry reads as the fulfilment of the word that God had made them contemptible and base (Malachi 2:9). Those could not but fear the people, he adds, who studied only how to make the people fear them.

The sharpest of Henry’s observations concerns what restrained them. The chief priests and elders were kept from an open denial of the truth, even against the conviction of their own minds, not by the fear of God but purely by the fear of the people. He then distinguishes two effects of that fear. The fear of man may bring good people into a snare (Proverbs 29:25); here it serves only to keep bad people from being overmuch wicked, since many bad people would be much worse than they are if they durst. Their calculation weighed not truth against falsehood but credit against safety. The same dread that had once kept ordinary believers from confessing Christ openly now grips the rulers, so that the shepherds tremble before the flock they ought to have led.
27:
Barnes will not let the answer pass as modesty: it was a direct falsehood, since they could have told, and what they should have said was that they would not tell. Clarke makes the same correction and supplies the suppressed reasoning, that in the words of truth it should have been we will not tell, for we will not have this man for the Messiah, because if we acknowledge John as his forerunner we must of necessity receive Jesus as the Christ. Gill points out how far this was from their ordinary practice, since at other times they took upon themselves to judge of a prophet whether he were true or false, and now, contrary to their office and character, declare they did not know. Henry catches the irony of the outcome, that when they would not confess their knowledge they were constrained to confess their ignorance, and remarks that there are many more afraid of the shame of lying than of the sin.

Ellicott reads the answer as a forfeiture rather than a retreat, calling the confession of impotence a virtual abdication. Before such a tribunal the Prophet whom they called in question might well refuse to plead, and in truth there was no need to answer at all; for those who were not wilfully blind and deaf, the words he had spoken, the works he had done and the sinless life he had led were already proofs of an authority from God.

The refusal that follows is therefore just rather than evasive. Men obstinately prejudiced against the strongest conviction are not fit to be discoursed with concerning Christ’s authority, and to argue further would be to cast pearls before swine. Henry grounds the silence in a principle that cuts wider than the scene: those who imprison the truths they know in unrighteousness, neither professing nor practising them, are justly denied the further truths they inquire after (Romans 1:18). Clarke adds the warning in its sharpest form, that God often hides from the wise and prudent what he reveals unto babes, so that men who use their wisdom only to invent excuses for rejecting the truth are punished with the very ignorance to which, in their own defence, they are obliged to have recourse.
28:
Henry describes the method before the matter. Reproving parables are appeals to the offenders themselves, judging them out of their own mouths, as Nathan’s did before David (2 Samuel 12:1). Pseudo-Chrysostom marvels at the boldness of it, that those who are to be judged in this cause are applied to as judges, and notes the technique that makes it work: Christ veils the allusion so that they might not perceive they were passing sentence on themselves.

On the imagery there is little disagreement. The father is God, who created all men, a common Father to all mankind, as Pseudo-Chrysostom and Henry both have it. The vineyard is the work which God requires man to do, which Henry characterises as vineyard work, creditable, profitable and pleasant. Today means during this present age, and carries the demand for present obedience, since the night comes when no man can work.

The two sons divide the interpreters. Jerome and Pseudo-Chrysostom take the first, who refuses and then repents, for the Gentiles, and the second, who promises and then fails, for the Jews who said at Sinai that all the Lord had spoken they would do (Exodus 24:3). Jerome records a simpler alternative, reading the pair as the righteous and sinners, the publicans who repented under John set against the Pharisees who only made a show of righteousness. Origen frames it more generally still, against those who promise great things and do none of them, and is careful to add that the Jews are not shut out, since when the fulness of the Gentiles has entered in all Israel shall be saved (Romans 11:25). Pseudo-Chrysostom, having offered the Gentile and Jewish scheme, then finds it strained on its own terms, publicans and harlots being themselves Jews, and settles instead on the common sort proving better than the Priests, the penitent people against the impenitent rulers. Calvin gathers the purpose of the whole: Christ unmasks those hypocrites, that they may no longer boast of being the ministers of God. A textual question runs under the readings, and Jerome takes a side, insisting the correct copies put the refusing son first, so that the hearers might be condemned by their own sentence, though some manuscripts reverse the order.
29:
Ellicott hears in the blunt refusal the rough recklessness of the classes the first son figures, the publicans and harlots, whose whole life up to the time of their conversion had been an open refusal to keep God’s laws. Clarke generalises it into the standing answer of the unconverted heart, calling it the reply of every sinner to the invitations of God, in which the Most High is treated without ceremony or respect. Gill presses it into a doctrine of the will: where, he asks, is man’s free will, since this is the true picture of it, and man has naturally no will to that which is good until grace turns him.

The turn in the verse is the word for the change of mind, and here the grammarians are careful. Robertson stresses that metamelētheis really means to repent in the sense of being sorry afterwards, and must be sharply distinguished from the verb and noun used at Matthew 3:2 and Matthew 3:8; it denotes a sorrow that may pass into true repentance or may end in remorse. Ellicott agrees that it expresses rather the regretful change of purpose than an entire transformation of character, the first stage of repentance, which may rise higher or may, as with Judas, who is described by the same word (Matthew 27:3), end only in remorse and despair. In this son the sorrow bore fruit: he got sorry for his stubborn refusal, and went and obeyed, which is what Paul means by saying that godly sorrow leads to repentance (compare 2 Corinthians 7:9).

Henry finds in the first son the pattern of grace toward the openly rebellious, observing that there are many who in the beginning are wicked and wilful and very unpromising, who afterward repent and mend, and reaching for Paul’s reminder that such were some of you (1 Corinthians 6:11). The proof of repentance for past resistance is in the one thing the son actually did, which was to comply and set to work — better late than never. Measured by that test the son who said no and went had done the father’s will more truly than fair words could, obedience being reckoned not by the promise of the lips but by the labour of the hands.
30:
The courteous answer is read as outward respect without substance. Ellicott finds the tone of it, contrasted with the rude refusal of the elder son, eminently characteristic as representing the surface religion of the Pharisees. Calvin traces the idiom to its origin, the phrase being borrowed from the Hebrew, in which a man offering his services says here I am, sir. He is careful not to let the parable be turned into a commendation of hesitation. Prompt obedience is a laudable virtue in itself, and Christ does not here give the commendation to slowness; but since both are improper, to delay before doing your duty and to promise what you do not perform, Christ shows that this hypocrisy is less to be endured than the fierceness which in process of time is subdued.

The whole failure lies in the two words that follow the promise. Clarke laments what a multitude of such are in the world, professing to know God but denying him in their works, and asks what such professions will avail when God comes to take away the soul. Wesley applies it to the men standing in front of Christ: just so did the scribes and Pharisees, who professed the greatest readiness and zeal in the service of God, and whose profession was bare, contradicted by all their actions.

Henry deepens the warning by describing how the failure happens rather than merely naming it. There are many who give good words and make fair promises in religion, and who rest there and go no further, and so come to nothing; saying and doing are two things, which is precisely the fault charged on the Pharisees (Matthew 23:3). Many with their mouth show much love while their heart goes another way, and the breaking point comes when they meet something to be done that is too hard or something to be parted with that is too dear, at which their good purposes prove to be to no purpose. Henry’s summary image is the one that sticks: buds and blossoms are not fruit. On that reading the second son, fair in word and barren in deed, is the more dangerous of the two, since a surface devotion hardens more easily than an open refusal.
31:
Gill notes whose verdict this is: the question is put by Christ on the strength of the preceding parable, and put to the chief priests, elders and scribes themselves, who answer it in their own persons. Barnes grants that the verdict was correct, and then registers the oddity that they did not perceive it condemned themselves. Ellicott presses the irony harder: the sentence came apparently from the lips of the very persons self-condemned by it, in something like an unconsciousness that they were being described in the person of the second son. Men who gave God thanks that they were not like other men could not imagine for an instant that the failure to go represented their own spiritual life. Henry explains why the first son is preferred, on grounds that have nothing to do with his manners: his actions were better than his words and his latter end than his beginning, which agrees with God’s own declared rule of judgment, that if the sinner turn from his wickedness he shall be pardoned (Ezekiel 18:21).

Then comes the reversal. Robertson renders the saying as the publicans and harlots marching ahead of the ecclesiastics into the kingdom, and calls it a powerful indictment of the complacency of the Jewish theological leaders. Ellicott finds a mercy hidden in the verb, which literally means to lead the way into, and reads it as implying that there was still time for scribes and Pharisees to follow in the rear: the door was not yet closed against them, though those whom they despised had taken the place of honour.

The two classes named are, Ellicott observes, purposely general, describing the action of classes rather than of individuals, and yet he cannot help associating them with the personal instances the Gospels supply — the publican who became an Apostle (Matthew 9:9), Zacchaeus (Luke 19:2), and the woman that was a sinner (Luke 7:37). Clarke draws the contrast in the terms of the parable. In all their former conduct these had said no, and now they yield to the voice of truth; the others, always professing the readiest obedience and pretending to wait for the kingdom of God, did not receive it when it came, choosing rather, while making the best professions, to continue members of the synagogue of Satan.
32:
The phrase describing John’s coming is read two ways. Ellicott takes it in a half-technical sense, expressing the aspect of righteousness which the Pharisees themselves recognised (Matthew 6:1) — the almsgiving, fasting and prayer conspicuous both in the life and in the teaching of the Baptist. Clarke construes the grammar differently, reading that John came to men who were themselves in the way of righteousness, the Jews standing within the way of revelation as the Gentiles did not. Henry uses the phrase as evidence of the question Christ had just asked, that John’s baptism was from heaven: by their fruits ye shall know them, and John taught people to repent and to work the works of righteousness, being himself a great example of strictness.

The success of the ministry seals the argument. Publicans are named among John’s hearers (Luke 3:12), and the women Ellicott takes to have felt the impulse of the strong popular movement (compare Luke 7:37). Henry turns the result into a proof: had God not sent John, he would not have crowned his labours with such wonderful success. Calvin will not let the believing be reduced to assent, insisting that faith does not consist solely in a person’s giving his agreement to true doctrine, but in the hearer renouncing himself and devoting his life wholly to God.

The sharpest word is the last clause, and Ellicott improves the rendering: they did not even repent afterward. The rulers were like the first of the two sons in his defiant refusal and unlike him in his subsequent repentance. What makes this the aggravation is the evidence they had in front of them; they were not even provoked to a holy emulation (Romans 11:14) by the spectacle of publicans and harlots going in before them. Calvin calls it an aggravated view of their malice, and the mark of people altogether depraved not to follow, at the very least, when publicans and harlots are the ones pointing out the road. Wesley closes with a sigh over his own century rather than the first, that this scripture is fulfilled at this day.
33:
The frame comes from Isaiah 5:1–7, where the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, as Jerome, Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Calvin all recognise. Origen marks the one decisive difference between the two: in Isaiah the threats are against the vineyard, where in the Gospel the husbandmen are blamed. That shift governs everything that follows.

The elements are read with broad agreement and variant detail. The householder is God, who Origen notes is in some parables represented as a man. Pseudo-Chrysostom distinguishes the titles, Father by goodness and Lord by nature. The vineyard is Israel, or as Henry has it the church, furnished with all things requisite. The hedge is read as the institutions which made Israel a separate people (Ellicott), the guardianship of Angels (Jerome), or God’s special protection (Henry). Barnes, Robertson and Ellicott prefer wine-vat to winepress; Henry takes it for the altar of burnt offerings, Ellicott for the Temple into which the wine of devotion was to flow. The tower is the Temple to Jerome, and Jerusalem with its outward polity to Ellicott. Hilary makes it the eminence of the Law, from which the coming of Christ might be spied. The husbandmen are the chief priests and elders. The far country Jerome refuses to treat as a change of place, since God, by whom all things are filled, cannot be absent; what the journey represents is his leaving the vine-dressers a freedom of acting.

Chrysostom is fullest on the design of the parable, and lists four things it shows at once: God’s providence exercised towards them from the first, their murderous disposition from the beginning, that the God of the New Testament and of the Old was one and the same, and finally the calling of the Gentiles with the casting out of the Jews. Calvin presses the stewardship instead. As God complained through Isaiah and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 2:21) that he received no fruit, so here he accuses the vine-dressers themselves, who like base swindlers appropriate the produce to their own use. Barnes alone urges restraint on the whole exercise: the circumstances serve to keep up the story, and where Christ has not explained them we have no right to press a meaning on each.
34:
Wesley identifies the two parties and keeps them distinct: the servants are God’s extraordinary messengers, the prophets, sent to the husbandmen, who are the ordinary preachers or ministers of the Jews. Barnes agrees that they represent the prophets sent to the Jewish people, and Clarke fills in what the errand was, since God sent them from time to time to call both priests and people back to the purity of his holy religion. Robertson draws attention to the distinction the parable itself maintains, the slaves being marked off from the husbandmen who had leased the vineyard; on his reading the conduct of the husbandmen towards the householder’s slaves portrays the behaviour of the Jewish people and their religious leaders towards the prophets, and now towards Christ.

The arrangement being described was an ordinary one. Barnes explains that the time of the fruit was the season of gathering, when the owner sent to receive the part that was his, the vineyard having been let out for a share of the produce. Clarke recognises in it the ancient custom of paying the rent of a farm in kind, still to be found in his own day in the highlands of Scotland. Gill brings in the law governing young trees, whose fruit was not to be eaten for the first years and was holy in the fourth (compare Leviticus 19:23–25).

Ellicott enters a caution against pressing the successive sendings too closely, on the honest ground that we cannot find any exact parallel in the history of Israel. It is enough, he says, to see in them the general expectation — the expectation Isaiah voices when God looked that his vineyard should bring forth grapes (Isaiah 5:4) — that the developed life of Israel should be worthy of its calling, together with the mission of the prophets who were sent from time to time to call the people to bring forth the fruits of righteousness. What the owner comes for, on every account given here, is not produce but the obedience of a people, rendered through the rulers entrusted with them; and that is why the refusal in the verses following is a refusal of something other than rent.
35:
Barnes begins with the first verb, which properly means to flay or to take off the skin, and so to whip in such a way that the skin is taken off in many places; Clarke and Lightfoot agree that it pictures scourging carried to excess. The second recalls a death by tradition, Isaiah being said to have been put to death by sawing him asunder. The third names the common Jewish penalty, inflicted on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, who was stoned in the court of the house of the Lord (2 Chronicles 24:21). Lightfoot sets the three verbs against the four kinds of death delivered to the Sanhedrim, which were stoning, burning, killing and strangling. Barnes and Ellicott then gather the wider testimony, that the prophets as a class had no light or easy task but were called upon one by one to suffer persecution (Hebrews 11:37; 2 Chronicles 36:16; Nehemiah 9:26), which is the charge Christ presses openly at Matthew 23:37.

Calvin reads the verse for what it shows about God rather than about the tenants. Where Mark and Luke name the servants one at a time, Matthew explains the matter more at large, namely that God, by sending a multitude of prophets, contended with the malice of the priests. Calvin’s image is military: God did not, on account of the cruelty of the priests, fail to send prophets, but raising them up as it were in troops, fought against their malice. The inference he draws runs the other way from comfort, since it measures how obstinate that malice was, for the correction of which no remedies were of any avail.

What the tenants return, then, is not merely no fruit but violence offered to the very mercy that came seeking it. Henry takes that for the standing pattern, what has all along been the lot of God’s faithful messengers, and adds the comparison that gives the parable its edge for anyone in office: if those who live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution, much more shall those who press others to it. The men set to gather fruit for God had become the fiercest enemies of the men he sent to collect it.
36:
Clarke objects to the usual rendering of the comparative, holding that the Greek should be read as more honourable rather than more than the first, and giving a reason for the preference: as the fullness of the time approached, each prophet more clearly and fully pointed out the coming of Christ, where more than the first conveys no meaning at all. Ellicott arrives at nearly the same sense without the textual argument, finding a reference to the greater power and fulness of the work of the later prophets, Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, stretching onward to the Baptist as the man who closed the whole line. Gill extends the second sending further down the history, suggesting it may take in those who suffered in the times of the Maccabees.
