Clarke draws from the repetition a doctrine of unceasing gift. There is not a moment in which God does not shower down his gifts upon men and require the fruit of them, and various instruments are used to bring sinners to God — prophets, apostles, pastors, teachers. He is equally unflinching about the constancy of the result: the true disciples of Christ have been persecuted in all ages, and the greatest share of the persecution has fallen upon the ministers of his religion, for there have always been good and bad husbandmen, and the latter have persecuted the former.

Henry sets the two persistencies side by side. On God’s part he marvels at the riches of the patience and forbearance that keep up in his church a despised and persecuted ministry, sending other servants, more than the first, though the first had sped no better. On the tenants’ part he explains the hardening by a rule about sin itself, that one sin makes way for another of the same kind. The escalating mercy and the deepening malice therefore run on together until the sending of the Son, each fresh embassy raising at once the privilege despised and the guilt incurred. That the second band, sent in greater fulness, met no better welcome than the first is the point the parable needs: the fault lay in no deficiency of means but wholly in the will of the husbandmen.
37:
This sending is the summit of the parable, and the other Gospels make it more tender still, Mark calling him one son, his beloved (Mark 12:6) and Luke putting the hope in the owner’s own mouth, that it may be they will reverence him (Luke 20:13). Ellicott reads the whole sequence as a gradually ascending scale of those who were sent, culminating in a difference not of degree only but of kind, like the contrast Hebrews draws between the prophets and the Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and finds in it the employment by God, in his long-suffering pity, of all possible means to lead his people to repentance. Barnes makes the verse a mirror of the gospel itself, beautifully and most tenderly exhibiting the love of God in sending his only Son to die for men (compare John 3:16; 1 John 4:9), one whom the world ought to reverence even as it should the Father.

The owner’s stated expectation raised an old difficulty, since God cannot be mistaken about what will happen. Calvin concedes the point and explains the idiom: strictly speaking the thought does not apply to God, who knew what would happen, but it is customary, especially in parables, to ascribe human feelings to him. He then argues that the clause was not added without reason, since it represents as in a mirror how deplorable their impiety was, that they rose in diabolical rage against the Son of God, who had come to bring them back to a sound mind. Clarke works from the verb, which he says means that they will reflect, and blush for shame because of it, when they see the son.

Henry presses what the Son brought that the servants could not. He comes with more authority, judgment being committed to him so that all men should honour him; reverence paid to him would have been a powerful and effectual principle of fruitfulness and obedience, and there is greater danger in refusing him than in despising Moses’ law. That the householder kept his Son until last is itself part of the argument, since it marks this as the final remedy, beyond which no further means remained to be tried.
38:
Several of the expositors insist the rulers knew whom they were killing. Lightfoot sets the verse beside John 11:48 and concludes that the rulers of the Jews acknowledged among themselves that Christ was the Messias, and put him to death nonetheless, lest by bringing in another worship and another people he should suppress their worship and themselves with it. Ellicott points to the counsel of Caiaphas that one man should die for the people (John 11:49), and to those who believed on him and yet through fear of the Pharisees were not confessed disciples (John 12:42); the parable, on his reading, showed them that they stood face to face with one who knew the secrets of their hearts. Gill distinguishes degrees of culpability, allowing that some were entirely ignorant while these men acted against light and conscience, with spite and malice.

What they coveted was not land. Robertson renders the plot as let us get his inheritance, marking the hortatory subjunctive, and Barnes observes the practical fact behind it, that the vineyard was rented to them and in their possession, and they resolved to keep it. Calvin supplies the motive from the verse before: the chief reason the priests raged against Christ was that they might not lose their tyranny, since he is the one by whom God chooses to govern.

Barnes enters his usual caution, that the detail has probably no reference to any particular conduct of the Jews and is thrown in to keep up the story. The others read it against the history, where the plot answers to the conspiracy Matthew records (Matthew 27:1), and the title heir answers to the prophetic promise that God would give him the heathen for his inheritance. Raban glosses that sharply: an inheritance not left him by his Father when dying, but wonderfully purchased by his own death (compare Hebrews 1:2). Paul’s word that had they known it they would not have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8) is reconciled with the rulers’ knowing malice by distinguishing the blind instruments, Pilate and the Roman power, from the chief priests who recognised the heir and slew him to keep the vineyard their own.
39:
Gill takes the first act of the arrest in the garden, where they seized and laid hold of him in a rude and violent manner, as they had done to some of the servants before: a band of soldiers and officers sent by the chief priests and Pharisees, who with swords and staves took him, bound him and led him away. Barnes refers the whole verse to the conduct of the Jews in putting the Saviour to death, by giving him into the hands of the Romans and seeking his crucifixion (compare Acts 2:23; Acts 7:52), and marks the sequence, that they put him to death after they had already persecuted and slain the prophets. He notes too that the hearers took the parable the same way, as the chapter’s closing verses show (v.45).

The order of the two acts is what the commentators find most telling. Barnes and Ellicott see a latent reference to the facts in the casting out before the slaying, since our Lord was delivered over to the judgment of the Gentiles and was crucified outside the Holy City (John 19:20; Hebrews 13:12), the vineyard standing in a special sense for Jerusalem as the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts. Christ was crucified out of the city, on Mount Calvary (Luke 23:33), cast out as though he were the shame and reproach of his people when he was in truth their greatest glory. Henry presses the same correspondence and completes it: they reckoned him unworthy to live, thrust him out of the holy city, and crucified him without the gate, so that as men had dealt with the servants they dealt at last with the Son.

Clarke turns the verse inward, away from the history and onto every impenitent hearer. To cast him out of the vineyard is to reject the counsel of God utterly, acknowledging neither the authority of Christ nor submitting to his teaching; and the motive he assigns is not malice but the wish to be left alone, since a sinner, to enjoy a little longer his false peace, rejects Jesus and persecutes the Gospel that troubles his sinful repose. On that reading the husbandmen’s last crime is both a thing foretold in the parable and enacted within the week, and also a thing repeated wherever the same quiet preference is made.
40:
Gill reads the owner’s arrival as God moving in a way of providence to call these husbandmen to account, and itemises the charges: not only the fruit they were to bring him, but their barbarity to his servants the prophets, time after time, and especially the inhuman usage and murder of his own son. Barnes states what the question was for, and it was not for information. Jesus asked them about the proper way of dealing with such men so that they might condemn themselves, and admit the justice of the punishment soon coming upon them.

Henry draws out both the certainty of the reckoning and the shrewdness of the appeal. The question assumes an owner who returns and settles accounts. God holds that title in fact, the ground belongs to him, and he will make it plain to men who now lord it over his heritage as though the whole were theirs. Against persecutors who say in their hearts that he delays his return, Henry sets a warning and a consolation together: though he bear long with them he will not bear always, and abused saints and ministers may reckon the Lord at hand, the Judge standing before the door.

The form of the question belongs, on Henry’s account, to the same method Nathan used with David, who pronounced sentence on the man in the story before he understood he was sentencing himself: God’s proceedings are so unexceptionable that there needs but an appeal to sinners themselves concerning the equity of them. By requiring the rulers to pronounce the sentence, Christ ensures that knowing the judgment of God against those who do such things they should be the more inexcusable, so that whatever they answered they would be justified in condemning the very wickedness that was their own. Henry closes with the observation that gives the device its force, that many can easily prognosticate the dismal consequences of other people’s sins who do not see what will be the end of their own. Asked to judge the husbandmen, these men pronounced without flinching a doom they did not yet recognise as a description of themselves.
41:
Barnes observes that the answer was given according as they knew men would act and would act justly, the case being so clear that they could not answer otherwise, and yet they did not see the bearing of what they had admitted. Robertson catches the assonance in the Greek, kakous kakōs apolesei, which he renders he will put the wretches to a wretched death. Henry carries the destruction into history, as fulfilled upon the Jews in the miserable ruin brought on them by the Romans about forty years after this, and warns that it falls still on all who, having enjoyed the greatest share of church privileges, do not improve them.

The other husbandmen are taken by all of them for the Gentiles, the church to which the kingdom passes (compare Romans 11:11). Ellicott classes the whole answer with the speech of Caiaphas (John 11:49–51) as an unconscious prophecy, in which were wrapped up at once the destruction of the Holy City and the transfer to the Gentile Church of the privileges that had belonged to Israel.

A harmony question remains, since Luke reports that they said God forbid (Luke 20:16). Augustine offers two solutions, that of the listening multitudes some answered as Matthew relates and some as Luke, or that the words, being true, might well be said to have been spoken by him who is truth. Ellicott prefers a psychological reading, finding in the priests an affected horror by which they sought to disguise their conviction that the parable was meant for them. On either account the verdict they pronounced, destruction for the wicked and the vineyard given to the faithful, was at once their own sentence and an oracle of the gospel’s passage to the nations. Henry takes the comfort out of it that the parable leaves: God will have a church in the world notwithstanding the unworthiness and opposition of many who abuse the privileges of it, and if one people forfeit the vineyard, the Lord of the vineyard will not be robbed of its fruits but will sooner or later find faithful and true labourers.
42:
The quotation comes from Psalm 118:22–23, and Ellicott notes the detail that gives it its sting: it stands in the immediate context of the verse which had supplied the hosanna shouts of the multitude a few days before. Clarke takes its first reference to David, at first rejected by the Jewish rulers and afterwards chosen by the Lord to be the great ruler of his people, and Barnes insists it applies no less to Jesus. The builders Clarke identifies as the chief priests and elders with the doctors of the law, who had the oversight of the Jewish church, God’s building, and would not allow Christ a place in it. The stone rejected for want of comeliness (compare Isaiah 53:2) is Christ, whom God made the foundation of the church; the figure recurs across the New Testament (Acts 4:11; Romans 9:33; Ephesians 2:20; 1 Peter 2:7), and rests on Isaiah’s promise of a precious corner stone laid in Zion (Isaiah 28:16).

Ellicott adds a second application that the parable’s own logic suggests. In this setting the rejected stone passes over into the nation bringing forth the fruits, becoming the corner-stone of the great edifice of the Catholic Church; and he does not treat that as competing with the reading which makes Christ himself the stone (compare Ephesians 1:22), since the head of the body and the foundation of the building are the same person under two figures.

Calvin fastens on the clause about whose work this is, and reads the whole citation as a prediction of how the kingdom would be established: Christ would be placed on his throne by the wonderful power of God, contrary to the will of men, so that however fiercely he may be assailed by those who appear to possess honour and dignity, he will nevertheless remain in his own rank. Two consequences follow for Calvin, and he states them as pastoral rather than speculative. We need not be perplexed by the wicked attempts of men, God having warned us beforehand what to expect; and in the setting up of Christ’s kingdom his power will prove victorious. Robertson sums the verse as a withering indictment: these experts in building God’s temple had rejected the corner-stone chosen by God, and God has the last word.
43:
Barnes states the sentence without softening it. The Jews had been the children of the kingdom, God’s chosen and peculiar people, and now the privilege was to be taken away and the blessing given to a nation that would bring forth the fruits of it, which is to say the Gentiles (Acts 28:28). Clarke reads the fruits as the returns of grace: as the parable alludes to paying a landlord in kind, so here the Gentiles are represented as paying God in kind, since nothing can ever be acceptable in God’s sight that does not spring from himself. Robertson calls the words the death-knell of the Jewish nation with their hopes of political and religious world leadership.

Calvin notices a shift in the address, that Christ now turns from the rulers to the people themselves, who had been the companions and assistants of the priests and scribes in hindering the grace of God. He then refuses to let the threat stay in the first century: it was once spoken to them and written for the sake of all of us, lest we grow wanton through a vain and wicked confidence in the flesh. The argument he builds on it runs from the greater to the lesser. If God spared not the natural branches (Romans 11:21), what will he do with those that were engrafted? Much less is the kingdom of God bound to us, if it be not rooted in true godliness.

The same verse yields Calvin his consolation, and he draws it from the permanence of what is being transferred rather than from any security in those who receive it. The perpetuity of that kingdom may afford comfort to all the godly, since though the ungodly destroyed the worship of God among themselves they would never cause the name of Christ to be abolished; God will find elsewhere a dwelling and habitation for his kingdom. The practical lesson he ends on is the parable’s own test: the Gospel is not preached in order that it may lie barren and inoperative, but that it may yield fruit — the very fruit the husbandmen withheld, and which the new nation was to render in its seasons.
44:
Two degrees of ruin are being described, and the distinction turns on which of the two is moving. To fall on the stone is to stumble at Christ in his humiliation, which Ellicott glosses as the offence taken at the outward lowliness of him who came as the carpenter’s son, an allusion to the stone of stumbling at Isaiah 8:14–15. Such a fall brought pain and humiliation with it and yet was not irretrievable, since the bruise might be healed, and it was the work of the Christ to heal it. Jerome reads the clause the same way, that the stumbler is broken and yet not altogether crushed, but preserved to salvation through endurance. For the stone to fall on a man is another matter. Ellicott marks the rapid transition to the very words of Daniel 2:34–35 and 44, and the verb that follows means to winnow and scatter as chaff, so that what is described is the destruction of all that resists Christ’s kingdom (compare Matthew 16:18).

Lightfoot, Barnes and Clarke anchor the image in the manner of Jewish execution, describing the stoning-scaffold built twice the height of a man, from which the culprit was cast down upon a stone; if he died of the fall, well, and if not, the second witness threw a heavy stone upon his heart. Robertson reaches for a modern equivalent, likening the shattering to a motor-car dashed against a stone wall. Clarke and Robertson both record the textual question, that the verse is wanting in the Codex Bezae and in Origen, while standing firm in the parallel at Luke 20:18.

Calvin draws the pastoral edge, beginning from what the rejection costs Christ, which is nothing: he suffers no loss when the wicked reject him, but by his own hardness he will break them, and will be the more highly glorified in their destruction. The doctrine therefore does two things at once. It instructs us to give ourselves up gently, with a mild and tractable heart, to the dominion of Christ, and it fortifies us against the obstinacy of the wicked, for whom a dreadful end is waiting. Gill adds the limit that keeps the first clause from frightening the wrong people, since it is spoken not of believers, whose stumbling is healed, but of those to whom Christ is a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence.
45:
The recognition was unmistakable, and Robertson reads the verb as ingressive: there was no mistaking the meaning of these parables, and the dullest could see the point. Jerome puts the same observation as a concession about their hardness, that hard as the hearts of the Jews were in unbelief, they yet perceived the Lord’s sentence was directed against themselves. Ellicott describes the change in their bearing, the real or affected unconsciousness of the drift of our Lord’s teaching being at last broken through, so that they were roused to a passionate desire for revenge.

Pseudo-Chrysostom turns the moment into a diagnosis of how guilty men receive reproof. The good man, taken in a sin, has sorrow because he has sinned; the bad man is grieved not because he has sinned but because he is found out, and he not only does not repent but is indignant with the man who reproved him. That is why, on his reading, these men being taken in their sins were stirred up to still greater wickedness. Raban finds the same scene acted daily in the Church, when a man who is a brother only in name is ashamed or afraid to assail the unity of faith and peace that he does not love, because of the good men among whom he lives.

Origen distinguishes two ways of laying hands on Jesus, the rulers’ murderous grasp and the Bride’s longing in the Song, who held him and would not let him go (Song of Solomon 3:4), and adds the comfort that the word of truth none can seize, nor put it to death. Calvin finds the verse instructive for every age, since it is impossible but that the rage of ungodly men will be more and more inflamed by threatenings, the word working on bad consciences like a hot iron. His conclusion is a prayer rather than a judgment: we ought to pray that God would subdue us to voluntary fear, lest the mere knowledge of his vengeance exasperate us the more. The recognition that should have driven these men to repentance drove them to fury instead, which is the surest evidence that the word had found its mark.
46:
Gill describes a malice held in check rather than abandoned. They did not by any outward action apprehend him, but secretly wished and earnestly desired to, being so irritated and provoked that they could scarcely keep their hands off him. Barnes puts the restraint down to one cause, that they would have gratified their malice at once but they feared the people, who took him for a prophet (compare Luke 7:16; John 7:40). Ellicott recalls that they had once before made a like attempt and had been baffled (John 7:44); now, with the Prophet surrounded by his own disciples and by an admiring crowd, they dared not use open violence and had to fall back upon the more crooked paths of stratagem and treachery.

Clarke draws the moral of a restraint that comes from the wrong motive: he who abstains from certain evils only through fear of scandal or punishment has already committed them in his heart, and is guilty before God. Against that he sets the intrepidity of our Lord, who in the very face of his most inveterate enemies bears a noble testimony to the truth, reproves their iniquities, denounces the Divine judgments and braves danger and death. The comparison he ends on is addressed to ministers rather than to rulers: a true minister of Christ fears nothing but God where his glory is concerned, and a hireling fears everything except the one he ought to fear.

Clarke also uses the close of the chapter to answer a charge brought against Christ, that of secular ambition. Through these five days in Jerusalem he spent his time teaching, precisely in the same way he had done for three years past, lodging nightly at Olivet and taking no notice of the royal honours the people had paid him beyond showing that an important prophecy was thereby fulfilled (Isaiah 62:11; Zechariah 9:9). His aim throughout, on Clarke’s account, was to call the people back to purity and holiness. So the chapter ends with the King unharmed, the rulers driven to plot in secret, and the conflict of the last week fully joined.
